hints: Think about the two elements named in the word hydro-carbon and what the word only means for other elements like oxygen or chlorine.
walkthrough:
Break the word apart**
Think hydro for hydrogen and carbon for carbon. A hydrocarbon is built from just those two elements. If oxygen, nitrogen, halogen or any other atom is present, it is no longer a hydrocarbon, even if it contains C and H.
Final answer: A compound or molecule containing carbon and hydrogen atoms only.

hints: Recall where mixtures of hydrocarbons such as petrol, diesel and naphtha are separated from by fractional distillation.
walkthrough:
Link naphtha to its source**
Naphtha is not made from scratch in a lab. It is one of the fractions obtained when crude oil is separated by fractional distillation. So the raw material you start with is crude oil itself.
Final answer: Crude oil (petroleum).

hints: Focus on the conditions, heated at high pressure in the absence of air, and that a long alkane $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$ is broken into smaller alkenes plus a smaller alkane.
walkthrough:
Recognise the cracking pattern**
You start with a long saturated alkane, $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$, and heat it strongly without air to split it into smaller molecules including ethene and propene. Breaking a large alkane into smaller alkanes and alkenes in this way is cracking, here thermal cracking because of the high temperature and pressure.
Final answer: (Thermal) cracking.

hints: Use atom balance: subtract the atoms in one ethene $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4$ and one propene $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$ from $\text{C}_{10}\text{H}_{22}$ to find the formula of W.
walkthrough:
Balance atoms to find W**
Equal moles means 1 mol of V gives 1 mol ethene + 1 mol propene + 1 mol W. Count carbons: $10 - 2 - 3 = 5$. Count hydrogens: $22 - 4 - 6 = 12$. So W is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$.

Use the straight chain saturated clue**
W is described as straight chain and saturated, so it must be unbranched pentane: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$. Draw all five carbons in a row with full displayed or structural bonds.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_3(\text{CH}_2)_3\text{CH}_3$ straight chain pentane, $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}$.

hints: Recall which acidic organic functional group is strong enough to react with $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3(aq)$ to release bubbles of gas.
walkthrough:
Connect fizzing to acidity**
Effervescence with sodium carbonate means an acid is releasing $\text{CO}_2$ gas. Alkenes, alcohols and most other groups do not do this. Propene oxidised to give two functional groups including one that fizzes with carbonate must contain a carboxylic acid group, $\text{COOH}$.
Final answer: Carboxylic acid group, $\text{CO}_2\text{H}$ / $\text{COOH}$.

hints: Recall the standard test for unsaturation with $\text{C=C}$ that involves addition across the double bond at room temperature.
Remember the colour change from orange brown to colourless that shows the reagent has been consumed.
walkthrough:
Choose the alkene test**
To prove $\text{C=C}$ is still present in X, add aqueous bromine, $\text{Br}_2(aq)$, often called bromine water. The $\text{Br-Br}$ adds across the double bond in an electrophilic addition.

State the colour change precisely**
Before mixing the solution is orange or brown. After shaking with an alkene the bromine is used up, so the colour disappears and the solution turns colourless. That decolourisation is the positive result.
Final answer: Add $\text{Br}_2(aq)$ / bromine water. Orange / brown solution decolourises to colourless.

hints: Look at the repeat unit backbone with two carbons in brackets and imagine reversing addition polymerisation by restoring the $\text{C=C}$ double bond.
walkthrough:
Work backwards from polymer to monomer**
In an addition polymer the repeat unit $-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}(X)-$ comes from a monomer $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH}(X)$. Here the side group X is $\text{C(=O)O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$.

Draw the monomer**
Put back the double bond between the two backbone carbons. You get sodium propenoate, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCOONa}$. Show the $\text{C=C}$ clearly and the full $\text{COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$ group.
Final answer: $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCOONa}$ / $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH(COO}^{-}\text{Na}^{+})$ displayed as $\text{CH}_2\text{=CH-C(=O)-O}^{-}\text{Na}^{+}$.

hints: Think about the carbon containing gas always formed when a carbon based polymer burns completely in oxygen and which is linked to global warming.
walkthrough:
Pick the greenhouse gas from combustion**
Polymer Z contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen plus sodium. Complete combustion in plenty of air converts all carbon to carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$. This is the main combustion gas that traps infrared radiation and enhances the greenhouse effect.
Final answer: Carbon dioxide, $\text{CO}_2$.

hints: Consider what toxic gas forms when carbon burns with limited oxygen, or what unburned fragments escape, and what harm each causes apart from warming.
walkthrough:
Identify a second harmful product**
Pure Z will not always burn perfectly, especially as a solid polymer. In limited oxygen, carbon forms carbon monoxide, $\text{CO}$, instead of $\text{CO}_2$. Unburned hydrocarbon fragments can also escape.

Link it to a non greenhouse harm**
Carbon monoxide is highly toxic because it binds to haemoglobin and prevents oxygen transport. Alternatively, released hydrocarbons help catalyse the formation of photochemical smog which irritates eyes and lungs. Either pair earns the mark.
Final answer: Gas: carbon monoxide, $\text{CO}$; consequence: toxic / poisonous, reduces oxygen transport in blood. OR Gas: hydrocarbons; consequence: contributes to photochemical smog.
